exercises.title: Rounding in a 3-digit system
exercises.description: Round to the nearest machine number in the toy system ($b = 10$, $t = 3$): (a) $123.456$, (b) $0.0004567$, (c) $9.996$. State mantissa and exponent each time.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Normalise ($1 \le m < 10$) and then round the mantissa to $t = 3$ digits.

Step 3: (c) Carry-over
$9.996 \to 10.0$ has to be renormalised: $1.00 \cdot 10^{1}$. Mantissa $1.00$, exponent $1$.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
First normalise, then round – and renormalise after rounding if necessary.

exercises.title: Absolute and relative error
exercises.description: The number $x = \sqrt{2} = 1.41421356\ldots$ is approximated by $\tilde x = 1.41$. Compute the absolute and the relative error.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Absolute: $|\tilde x - x|$. Relative: $|\tilde x - x| / |x|$.

Step 3: Relative error
$0.00421356 / 1.41421356 \approx 2.98 \cdot 10^{-3}$, i.e. about $0.3\,\%$.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
The relative error puts the error in proportion to the size of the number – it is the more meaningful quantity.

exercises.title: Binary to decimal
exercises.description: Convert $(101.011)_2$ into a decimal number.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Place values: left of the point $2^2, 2^1, 2^0$, right of it $2^{-1}, 2^{-2}, 2^{-3}$.

Step 2: Add up
$1 \cdot 4 + 0 \cdot 2 + 1 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot \tfrac12 + 1 \cdot \tfrac14 + 1 \cdot \tfrac18 = 4 + 1 + 0.25 + 0.125$.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
Finite binary fractions are exactly the decimals of the form $k/2^n$ – that is why $0.375 = 3/8$ is exact but $0.1$ is not.

exercises.title: Largest and smallest machine number
exercises.description: A toy system has $b = 10$, $t = 3$ and exponents $e \in \{-4, \dots, 4\}$. Find the largest and the smallest positive normalised machine number.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Largest number: largest mantissa and largest exponent. Smallest positive number: smallest normalised mantissa and smallest exponent.

Step 2: Largest number
Mantissa $9.99$, exponent $4$: $x_{\max} = 9.99 \cdot 10^{4} = 99900$.

Step 3: Smallest positive number
Mantissa $1.00$, exponent $-4$: $x_{\min} = 1.00 \cdot 10^{-4}$.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
The mantissa of a normalised number lies in $[1, b)$, so never below $1.00$.

exercises.title: Computing machine epsilon
exercises.description: Compute $\varepsilon_{\text{mach}} = b^{1-t}$ and $u = \tfrac12 \varepsilon_{\text{mach}}$ for the system $b = 2$, $t = 24$ (IEEE single precision).
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$\varepsilon_{\text{mach}}$ is the distance from $1$ to the next machine number, $u$ the unit roundoff.

Step 2: Plug in
$\varepsilon_{\text{mach}} = 2^{1-24} = 2^{-23} \approx 1.19 \cdot 10^{-7}$.

Step 3: Unit roundoff
$u = 2^{-24} \approx 5.96 \cdot 10^{-8}$. Single precision therefore has about 7 significant decimal digits.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
$\varepsilon_{\text{mach}}$ is not a “smallest value” but the relative resolution at $1$.

exercises.title: Counting machine numbers
exercises.description: How many machine numbers (including $0$) does the system with $b = 2$, $t = 3$ and exponents $e \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$ have?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Count signs, mantissas and exponents and add the $0$.

Step 2: Mantissas
Normalised: $1.d_1 d_2$ with $d_1, d_2 \in \{0,1\}$ – that is $4$ mantissas: $1.00,\ 1.01,\ 1.10,\ 1.11$.

Step 3: Count
$2 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 = 24$ nonzero numbers, plus the $0$: $25$ in total.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
There are only finitely many machine numbers – that is the root of all rounding problems.

exercises.title: Normalising
exercises.description: Write $0.00372$, $5280$ and $-0.1$ in normalised form $\pm m \cdot 10^{e}$ with $1 \le m < 10$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Shift the point so that exactly one nonzero digit stands before it; the exponent counts the shift.

Step 2: The three numbers
$0.00372 = 3.72 \cdot 10^{-3}$ (point moved 3 places right). $5280 = 5.28 \cdot 10^{3}$. $-0.1 = -1.0 \cdot 10^{-1}$.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
Shifting the point left ⇒ larger exponent, right ⇒ smaller.

exercises.title: Why fl(1 + 10^-17) = 1
exercises.description: Explain why $\mathrm{fl}(1 + 10^{-17}) = 1$ holds in double precision.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Check which machine number $1 + 10^{-17}$ is closest to.

Step 2: Neighbour of 1
The next machine number after $1$ is $1 + 2^{-52} \approx 1 + 2.2 \cdot 10^{-16}$.

Step 3: Compare distances
$1 + 10^{-17}$ is $10^{-17}$ away from $1$ but almost $2.2 \cdot 10^{-16}$ from its neighbour. It is less than $u \approx 1.1 \cdot 10^{-16}$ away from $1$, so it is rounded to $1$.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
A summand smaller than $u \cdot |\text{main sum}|$ is lost completely.

exercises.title: Summing in two orders
exercises.description: In the toy system ($b = 10$, $t = 3$) compute $1000 + 4 + 4$ (a) as $(1000 + 4) + 4$ and (b) as $1000 + (4 + 4)$. Compare with the exact value and state the errors.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
After every operation round to $3$ digits. Exact: $1008$.

Step 2: (a) from the left
$\mathrm{fl}(1000 + 4) = \mathrm{fl}(1004) = 1.00 \cdot 10^{3} = 1000$. Then $\mathrm{fl}(1000 + 4) = 1000$. Result $1000$, error $8$.

Step 3: (b) small ones first
$\mathrm{fl}(4 + 4) = 8$, then $\mathrm{fl}(1000 + 8) = \mathrm{fl}(1008) = 1.01 \cdot 10^{3} = 1010$. Error $2$.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
Associativity does not hold in floating point. Adding the small summands first gives the smaller error here.

exercises.title: Quantifying cancellation
exercises.description: The exact numbers $x = 2.718282$ and $y = 2.718271$ are rounded to $5$ significant digits. Compute $x - y$ exactly and with the rounded values and determine the relative error of the result.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Round both numbers, subtract and compare with the exact difference.

Step 2: Exact and rounded
Exact: $x - y = 0.000011$. Rounded: $\tilde x = 2.7183$, $\tilde y = 2.7183$, so $\tilde x - \tilde y = 0$.

Step 3: Error
Relative error of the result: $|0 - 0.000011| / 0.000011 = 100\,\%$. The inputs only had a relative error $\le 1.9 \cdot 10^{-5}$.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
Cancellation amplifies tiny relative input errors into large relative result errors – here by a factor of about $10^{4}$–$10^{5}$.

exercises.title: Rewriting a root difference
exercises.description: Compute $\sqrt{x+1} - \sqrt{x}$ for $x = 10^{6}$ in $6$-digit arithmetic (a) directly, (b) after rewriting with the conjugate sum.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$\sqrt{x+1}$ and $\sqrt{x}$ are almost equal – cancellation looms. Multiplying by $\sqrt{x+1} + \sqrt{x}$ removes the subtraction.

Step 2: Directly
$\sqrt{1000001} = 1000.0005 \to 1000.00$ (6 digits), $\sqrt{10^{6}} = 1000.00$. Difference: $0$ – completely wrong.

Step 3: Rewritten
$\sqrt{x+1} - \sqrt{x} = \dfrac{(x+1) - x}{\sqrt{x+1} + \sqrt{x}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x+1} + \sqrt{x}} = \dfrac{1}{2000.00} = 5.00000 \cdot 10^{-4}$.

Step 4: Check
Exact: $4.99999875 \cdot 10^{-4}$. The rewritten computation is correct to $6$ digits.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Difference of two roots ⇒ multiply by the conjugate (difference of squares).

exercises.title: Binary expansion of 0.1
exercises.description: Expand $0.1$ in binary by repeated doubling and explain why $0.1$ cannot be stored exactly as a machine number.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Doubling: if the result is $\ge 1$ the digit is $1$ and you subtract $1$; otherwise the digit is $0$.

Step 3: Periodicity
The remainder $0.2$ repeats: $0.1 = (0.0\overline{0011})_2$. The expansion never terminates.

Step 4: Conclusion
A machine number has only $53$ mantissa digits. $0.1$ has to be rounded: what is stored is $0.1000000000000000055\ldots$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Decimal fractions usually have no finite binary expansion. Only numbers of the form $k/2^n$ are exactly representable.

exercises.title: Error propagation in a product
exercises.description: Let $\tilde x = x(1 + \delta_x)$ and $\tilde y = y(1 + \delta_y)$. Show that the relative error of the product satisfies $\delta_{xy} \approx \delta_x + \delta_y$ and check this for $x = 2$, $\tilde x = 2.02$, $y = 5$, $\tilde y = 4.9$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Multiply out the perturbed values and neglect second-order terms.

Step 2: Derivation
$\tilde x \tilde y = xy(1 + \delta_x)(1 + \delta_y) = xy(1 + \delta_x + \delta_y + \delta_x\delta_y)$. So $\delta_{xy} = \delta_x + \delta_y + \delta_x \delta_y \approx \delta_x + \delta_y$.

Step 3: Numerical example
$\delta_x = 0.02/2 = 0.01$, $\delta_y = -0.1/5 = -0.02$. Product: $2.02 \cdot 4.9 = 9.898$ instead of $10$, so $\delta_{xy} = -0.0102$.

Step 4: Comparison
$\delta_x + \delta_y = -0.01$; the term $\delta_x \delta_y = -0.0002$ explains the difference.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
In multiplication (and division) the relative errors add up – the operation is benign.

exercises.title: Vieta trick for the quadratic formula
exercises.description: Solve $x^2 - 1000x + 1 = 0$ in $5$-digit arithmetic (a) with the quadratic formula and (b) using Vieta's formula. The exact small root is $x_2 = 0.0010000010\ldots$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The minus in front of the root causes cancellation. Vieta: $x_1 x_2 = 1$.

Step 2: (a) Formula
$\sqrt{1000^2 - 4} = \sqrt{999996} = 999.998 \to 1000.0$ (5 digits). Then $x_2 = (1000 - 1000.0)/2 = 0$ – completely wrong.

Step 4: Comparison
The error is now only $10^{-9}$ absolute, about $10^{-6}$ relative – within the arithmetic precision.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Always compute the root without subtraction first, the other one via $x_1 x_2 = c/a$.

exercises.title: (1 − cos x)/x² for small x
exercises.description: Compute $f(x) = \dfrac{1 - \cos x}{x^2}$ for $x = 10^{-4}$ in $8$-digit arithmetic. Note $\cos(10^{-4}) = 0.99999999500\ldots$. Rewrite $f$ so that no cancellation occurs and state $\lim_{x\to 0} f(x)$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The cosine is so close to $1$ that $1 - \cos x$ vanishes in $8$ digits.

Step 2: Directly
$\cos(10^{-4}) \to 1.0000000$ (8 digits), so $1 - \cos x = 0$ and $f = 0$ – wrong.

Step 3: Rewriting
$1 - \cos x = 2\sin^2(x/2)$, so $f(x) = \dfrac{2\sin^2(x/2)}{x^2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{\sin(x/2)}{x/2}\right)^2$.

Step 4: Result
$\sin(x/2)/(x/2) \to 1$, so $f(10^{-4}) \approx 0.5$ and $\lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = \tfrac12$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Identities ($1 - \cos x = 2\sin^2\frac{x}{2}$) or Taylor series remove cancellation near $0$.

exercises.title: Error bound for fl(fl(a+b)+c)
exercises.description: For positive machine numbers $a, b, c$ the sum $s = a + b + c$ is computed as $\mathrm{fl}(\mathrm{fl}(a+b)+c)$. Show that the relative error is at most about $2u$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Apply the rounding rule $\mathrm{fl}(x \circ y) = (x \circ y)(1 + \varepsilon)$ twice.

Step 2: Two roundings
$\mathrm{fl}(a+b) = (a+b)(1+\varepsilon_1)$, then $\tilde s = \big((a+b)(1+\varepsilon_1) + c\big)(1+\varepsilon_2)$, $|\varepsilon_i| \le u$.

Step 3: Expanding
$\tilde s = (a+b+c) + (a+b)\varepsilon_1 + (a+b+c)\varepsilon_2 + O(u^2)$.

Step 4: Estimating
$\dfrac{|\tilde s - s|}{s} \le \dfrac{a+b}{a+b+c}u + u \le 2u$ since $a, b, c > 0$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
For positive summands the error grows only mildly with the number of additions – with mixed signs cancellation threatens.

exercises.title: Number of all machine numbers
exercises.description: Derive the number of all normalised machine numbers (including $0$) in the system $(b, t, e_{\min}, e_{\max})$ and check the formula for $b = 2$, $t = 3$, $e \in \{-1,0,1\}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Count independently: signs, mantissas, exponents – and do not forget the $0$.

Step 2: Mantissas
First digit $d_0 \in \{1, \dots, b-1\}$ ($b-1$ choices), the remaining $t-1$ digits free ($b^{t-1}$). Together $(b-1)\,b^{t-1}$ mantissas.

Step 3: Exponents and signs
Exponents: $e_{\max} - e_{\min} + 1$. Signs: $2$. The $0$ counts separately.

Step 5: Check
$b = 2$, $t = 3$: $N = 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 + 1 = 25$ – matches the direct count.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
Mantissas times exponents times signs; subnormals and special values (Inf, NaN) are not counted here.

exercises.title: Spacing and relative rounding error
exercises.description: Show: in $[b^{e}, b^{e+1})$ neighbouring machine numbers have spacing $b^{e+1-t}$. Conclude $|\mathrm{fl}(x) - x|/|x| \le \tfrac12 b^{1-t} = u$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The spacing is the place value of the last mantissa digit.

Step 2: Spacing
The mantissa $d_0.d_1\ldots d_{t-1}$ has last place value $b^{-(t-1)}$. Multiplied by $b^{e}$ this gives the spacing $b^{e}\cdot b^{1-t} = b^{e+1-t}$.

Step 3: Absolute rounding error
Rounding to the nearest machine number gives $|\mathrm{fl}(x) - x| \le \tfrac12 b^{e+1-t}$.

Step 4: Relative error
Because $|x| \ge b^{e}$ we get $\dfrac{|\mathrm{fl}(x) - x|}{|x|} \le \dfrac{\tfrac12 b^{e+1-t}}{b^{e}} = \tfrac12 b^{1-t} = u$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
The absolute spacing grows with $e$, the relative error stays bounded by $u$ – that is the idea of floating point.

exercises.title: Error of a sum of n numbers
exercises.description: The numbers $x_1, \dots, x_n > 0$ are added left to right: $s_k = \mathrm{fl}(s_{k-1} + x_k)$, $s_1 = x_1$. Show to first order $|s_n - \sum x_i| \le (n-1)\,u \sum x_i$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Track how many roundings each summand goes through.

Step 2: Recursion
$s_k = (s_{k-1} + x_k)(1 + \varepsilon_k)$, $|\varepsilon_k| \le u$, $k = 2, \dots, n$.

Step 3: Unrolling
$s_n = x_1 \prod_{k=2}^{n}(1+\varepsilon_k) + x_2 \prod_{k=2}^{n}(1+\varepsilon_k) + x_3 \prod_{k=3}^{n}(1+\varepsilon_k) + \dots + x_n (1 + \varepsilon_n)$. The summand $x_j$ carries $n - j + 1$ factors (for $j \ge 2$), $x_1$ carries $n-1$.

Step 4: Estimating
Each product is $1 + \theta$ with $|\theta| \le (n-1)u + O(u^2)$. Hence $|s_n - \sum x_i| \le (n-1)\,u \sum x_i$ (all $x_i > 0$).

Step 5: Improvement
The early summands are rounded most often. Sorting ascending makes the small summands the “often rounded” ones – which reduces the total error.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
The worst-case error grows linearly in $n$. In practice sorting, pairwise summation or Kahan summation helps.

exercises.title: Stable variance formula
exercises.description: For the data $x = (10^{8}+1,\ 10^{8}+2,\ 10^{8}+3)$ the variance (with factor $1/n$) is $\tfrac23$. Why does the textbook formula $\frac1n\sum x_i^2 - \bar x^2$ return nonsense (the result $0$) in double precision, and how do you compute it stably?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The textbook formula subtracts two huge, almost equal numbers (cancellation).

Step 2: Textbook formula
$\sum x_i^2 / n \approx 10^{16}$ and $\bar x^2 \approx 10^{16}$; both carry rounding errors of size $\approx 1$–$2$ (the spacing of machine numbers at $10^{16}$ is $2$). The difference should be $0.67$ – it is of the order of the rounding errors, here $0$.

Step 3: Stable variant
First the mean $\bar x = 10^{8} + 2$, then $\frac1n \sum (x_i - \bar x)^2$: deviations $-1, 0, 1$ are exact, $\frac13(1 + 0 + 1) = \frac23$.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
Centring before squaring prevents cancellation. The two-pass algorithm is stable, the one-pass formula is not (both solve the same, well-conditioned problem).

exercises.title: e^x − 1 for small x
exercises.description: Compute $f(x) = e^{x} - 1$ for $x = 10^{-10}$. Directly in double precision one obtains $1.00000008274\cdot 10^{-10}$. Explain the error and give a stable alternative.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
For $x \to 0$ we have $e^{x} \approx 1$ – subtracting $1$ cancels almost all digits.

Step 2: Error analysis
$e^{10^{-10}} = 1.0000000001\ldots$ is stored with relative error $\approx 10^{-16}$, i.e. absolute $10^{-16}$. After subtracting $1$ this absolute error sits next to $10^{-10}$: relative error $\approx 10^{-6}$ (here $8.3 \cdot 10^{-8}$).

Step 3: Stable alternative
Taylor series: $e^{x} - 1 = x + \tfrac{x^2}{2} + \tfrac{x^3}{6} + \dots$. For $x = 10^{-10}$: $10^{-10} + 5 \cdot 10^{-21} = 1.00000000005 \cdot 10^{-10}$ (correct to all digits).

Step 4: Library function
Computers provide a dedicated function (expm1) that uses exactly this idea internally.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
For small $|x|$ prefer a series expansion over a difference of nearly equal numbers.

exercises.title: Kahan summation
exercises.description: Explain the idea of Kahan summation and use it in the toy system ($b = 10$, $t = 3$) to compute $1000 + 4 + 4$. Compare with the exact value $1008$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The summation keeps in a helper variable $c$ what was lost when rounding and adds it back with the next summand.

Step 2: Algorithm
Start with $s = 0$, $c = 0$. For each summand $x$: (1) $y = x - c$; (2) $t = \mathrm{fl}(s + y)$; (3) $c = \mathrm{fl}(\mathrm{fl}(t - s) - y)$; (4) $s = t$.

Step 5: Second 4
$y = 4 - (-4) = 8$, $t = \mathrm{fl}(1008) = 1010$, $c = (1010 - 1000) - 8 = 2$, $s = 1010$. Result $1010$ instead of $1000$ – error $2$ instead of $8$; and $c = 2$ shows that $s$ is too large by $2$.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
Kahan summation keeps the error of the sum of order $u$ independent of $n$ (instead of $n u$) at little extra cost.

exercises.title: Underflow and the log trick
exercises.description: A model multiplies $400$ probabilities of size $0.01$. In double precision this gives $0$ (underflow, smallest positive number $\approx 10^{-308}$ or $5\cdot 10^{-324}$ subnormal). How do you compute it instead and how large is the result?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The product is $10^{-800}$ – far below the representable range. Taking logarithms turns the product into a sum.

Step 2: Logarithm
$\ln \prod p_i = \sum \ln p_i = 400 \cdot \ln 0.01 = 400 \cdot (-4.60517) \approx -1842.07$.

Step 3: Interpretation
The product is $e^{-1842.07} = 10^{-800}$. The number $-1842.07$ is easily representable; models are compared directly through their log values.

Step 4: Why this is stable
Each summand $\ln p_i$ has relative error $\approx u$, the sum grows only linearly. Underflow and overflow do not occur at all.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Always compute products of many small numbers (probabilities, likelihoods) as sums of logarithms.

exercises.title: ln(1 + x) for small x
exercises.description: Compute $\ln(1+x)$ for $x = 10^{-15}$. Directly one gets $1.1102\cdot 10^{-15}$ in double precision. Explain this and show that $\ln(u)\cdot x/(u-1)$ with $u = \mathrm{fl}(1+x)$ largely compensates the error.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The problem is the addition $1 + x$: it loses the lower digits of $x$.

Step 2: Loss in 1 + x
Machine numbers near $1$ have spacing $2.2\cdot 10^{-16}$. $1 + 10^{-15}$ is rounded to $u = 1.000000000000001 = 1 + 4.5\varepsilon_{\text{mach}}$, so $u - 1 = 1.11\cdot 10^{-15}$ instead of $10^{-15}$.

Step 3: Directly
$\ln u \approx u - 1 = 1.11\cdot 10^{-15}$: relative error $\approx 11\,\%$.

Step 4: Kahan trick
$\ln(1+x) = \dfrac{\ln(u)}{u-1}\cdot x$, because $\ln(u)/(u-1) \approx 1$ is insensitive to the rounding error in $u$ while $x$ enters exactly. Result $1.11\cdot 10^{-15} / 1.11\cdot 10^{-15} \cdot 10^{-15} \approx 10^{-15}$ (correct).

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Again: compensate the loss in $1 + x$ (Kahan) or use a special function (log1p) or the series $x - x^2/2 + \dots$.
